issues.item: Triggers: Victim Similarity: People who look similar to the victims
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma, 'people who look similar to the victims' is clinically incoherent because the patient is the victim; a plausible trigger would be people resembling the perpetrator(s) or contextual robbery cues. As written, this item conflicts with the trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Feeling dirty/contaminated is not impossible after robbery, but in this profile it is hard to reconcile with the rest of the selected items, which otherwise center on danger, self-blame, and moral injury rather than sexual violation or disgust-based trauma themes. This makes the appraisal set clinically inconsistent with the trauma context.

For a mugging/robbery trauma, 'Being naked' as a primary trigger is hard to reconcile unless there was a stripping/sexual humiliation element, which is not suggested elsewhere in the profile. The other trigger items point to perpetrator proximity and assault cues, making this vulnerability trigger clinically incongruent with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' implies morally troubling behaviour during the event, but the rest of the profile reflects victim-focused danger, self-blame, and mistrust rather than any specific morally injurious action. In a mugging/robbery context this item is difficult to justify without corroborating memory/appraisal content about the patient's own behaviour.

vignette:
Leilani, a 35-year-old accountant from a Pacific Islander background, had always taken pride in her careful, ordered life. That sense of order shattered one evening when she was leaving her office building in downtown Honolulu. As she walked toward her car, she heard footsteps quickening behind her. Before she could turn, a hand grabbed her shoulder and yanked her backward. She felt a cold blade press against her neck, tasted the metallic tang of her own blood where she’d bitten her tongue, and froze completely—her body locked in that twisted half-turn position. The man demanded her bag, then shoved her to the ground and ran. In the weeks that followed, Leilani could not shake the feeling that the attack had happened because of something fundamentally wrong with her. She found herself thinking, “This happened because of the kind of person I am,” and she became convinced the world was a dangerous place where no one could be trusted. She blamed herself for not walking faster, for not carrying pepper spray, for being too trusting. And the more she told herself she was to blame, the more the memory returned — as if her guilt needed to revisit the scene to confirm the verdict. These appraisals colored everything: every time she heard footsteps behind her, she was certain it was another threat, and she began to assume that any delay—her husband coming home late, a traffic light staying red too long—meant something terrible was happening. Even when her husband reassured her she was safe, she could not relax; she felt coiled, vigilant, unable to believe safety was real. When the threat felt this constant and this close, she found that scanning every face in a crowd before entering a room wasn't a symptom — it was just sensible, the only way she could move through her day without her heart hammering out of her chest. The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed. Living in that constant state of threat, she found that the memory would surface without warning — summoned by the adrenaline her body carried everywhere.

The memory of the mugging refused to settle. And because the memory was so vivid, it began to connect itself to things that had never been triggers before — a certain time of day, the smell of rain on asphalt — as if the memory was seeding its own reminders. When it surfaced, she would taste blood again, and her body would involuntarily stiffen into that same position, her shoulders twisted, her arms locked. The memory felt so extreme, so vivid, that she sometimes doubted it had actually happened to her—it felt like a nightmare she had overheard. These memory intrusions were almost always triggered by specific cues: footsteps approaching from behind, the sight of a man with a similar build wearing a grey hoodie, or an unexpected touch on her shoulder from a colleague or even her husband. Each of these cues brought with it not just fear, but a wave of self-blame — the thought that she should have known better, that she was the kind of person who drew danger. Each trigger plunged her back into the moment, and each time, the memory made her threat system spike—her heart pounded, and she became convinced that danger was imminent again. In response, she developed strategies she hoped would protect her. She would deliberately try to leave her body, blanking out when the memories came, as if observing herself from a distance. She also ruminated endlessly—dwelling on what she had done wrong, replaying the event to find a way it could have been prevented. But the more she replayed it, the more the memory intruded — all that mental rehearsal kept the scene polished and ready, as if each replay made the image sharper rather than duller. She would go over every second: if she had left five minutes earlier, if she had taken a different route. That rumination, however, only deepened her sense of blame, reinforcing her belief that she was the kind of person who brought disaster upon herself. And the more she blamed herself, the more hypervigilant she became, scanning every street, every sound—a cycle that made her feel even more unsafe. That hypervigilance meant that ordinary sounds — a car backfiring, a door closing too hard — now registered as potential threats, turning benign moments into triggers.

Her accountant job required long hours in a high-rise building with a parking garage. The walk from her desk to the elevator now triggered her daily: footsteps of coworkers behind her in the hallway made her flinch. She began taking the stairs to avoid people, but the echo of her own steps sounded like someone following her. At home, she could not let her husband touch her from behind; even a gentle hand on her shoulder made her jump and dissociate. She spent evenings dissociating in front of the TV, trying to blank out, but then the memories would loop again. The therapist she finally saw after months of deteriorating sleep and avoidance—she had stopped going to the grocery store after dark, stopped taking the bus—noted that Leilani had come to see her world as fundamentally treacherous, and that her own character was defective. What finally drove her to seek help was a panic attack in the office parking garage when a delivery driver’s footsteps echoed too close. She sat in her car, trembling, tasting blood, unable to move, and realized she could no longer live this way. She was terrified that she would never feel safe again, but she was even more afraid that the person she had become—the one who blamed herself for everything—was beyond repair. That conviction meant that almost anything could become a trigger — a stranger's glance held too long, a car door slamming — each one confirming her suspicion.

- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not show that triggers cause negative appraisals; triggers lead to threat and memory, but appraisals are not directly caused by triggers.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette shows memory causing appraisals via rumination, but not the reverse; negative appraisals do not directly cause memory intrusion.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not indicate negative appraisals cause triggers; triggers are external and independent of appraisals.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette shows triggers cause memory, not memory causing triggers; no causal relationship from memory to triggers.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette shows memory causing threat, but threat does not cause memory intrusions.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."

  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."

She sat in her car, trembling, tasting blood, unable to move, and realized she could no longer live this way. She was terrified that she would never feel safe again, but she was even more afraid that the person she had become—the one who blamed herself for everything—was beyond repair. That conviction meant that almost anything could become a trigger — a stranger's glance held too long, a car door slamming — each one confirming her suspicion.
